anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Measuring signal amplitude with the y-gain > Worked Example 1: Measuring signal amplitude: "We multiply the vertical divisions by the y-gain setting to find the peak voltage."
title: Extracting Signal Amplitude from a CRO Graticule
action: Select the correct signal amplitude in volts for a CRO trace extending 2.4 divisions vertically from the equilibrium centre line to a crest with a y-gain setting of 50 mV div^-1.
prompt: A sinusoidal electrical signal is displayed on an oscilloscope. The trace reaches a crest 2.4 divisions above the central equilibrium axis. The y-gain is set to 50 mV div^-1. What is the amplitude of the signal?

options.text: 0.12 V, calculated from V_0 = 2.4 div x (50 x 10^-3 V div^-1).
0.24 V, calculated from V_0 = 2 x 2.4 div x (50 x 10^-3 V div^-1).
120 V, calculated from V_0 = 2.4 div x 50 V div^-1 without prefix conversion.
0.048 V, calculated by dividing 2.4 div by 50 mV div^-1.

feedback.A: Correct. Amplitude is the peak voltage measured from the central equilibrium axis to a crest: V_0 = 2.4 div x 50 mV div^-1 = 120 mV = 0.12 V.
feedback.B: Incorrect. This calculation doubles the amplitude by computing peak-to-peak voltage. Amplitude is measured from the equilibrium centre line to a crest, not from trough to crest.
feedback.C: Incorrect. This calculation neglects the milli- prefix (10^-3). 50 mV corresponds to 0.050 V, yielding 0.12 V rather than 120 V.
feedback.D: Incorrect. Signal voltage is obtained by multiplying divisions by the y-gain setting, not by dividing.

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Measuring period and frequency with the time-base > Worked Example 2: Determining period and frequency: "Taking the reciprocal gives a frequency of 1250 Hz, which rounds to $1300\text{ Hz}$."
title: Determining Period and Frequency from Multi-Cycle Spans
action: Select the correct frequency for a wave whose trace spans 4 complete cycles across 10.0 cm with a time-base setting of 0.50 ms cm^-1.
prompt: Four complete wave cycles occupy a horizontal distance of 10.0 cm on a CRO screen. The time-base setting is 0.50 ms cm^-1. What is the frequency of the wave?

options.text: 800 Hz, because period T = (10.0 cm x 0.50 x 10^-3 s cm^-1) / 4 = 1.25 x 10^-3 s, and f = 1 / T = 800 Hz.
200 Hz, because T = 10.0 cm x 0.50 x 10^-3 s cm^-1 = 5.0 x 10^-3 s without dividing by cycle count.
1.25 x 10^-3 Hz, because the period value in seconds was reported directly as frequency.
3200 Hz, because the period of one cycle was multiplied by 4 instead of divided by 4.

feedback.A: Correct. The horizontal distance for one cycle is 10.0 cm / 4 = 2.5 cm. Period T = 2.5 cm x 0.50 ms cm^-1 = 1.25 ms = 1.25 x 10^-3 s. Frequency f = 1 / T = 1 / (1.25 x 10^-3 s) = 800 Hz.
feedback.B: Incorrect. This uses the total time across all 4 cycles (5.0 ms) as the period of a single cycle. You must divide the total span by 4 to obtain the period of one cycle.
feedback.C: Incorrect. 1.25 x 10^-3 s is the period T, not the frequency. Remember to take the reciprocal f = 1 / T to find frequency in hertz.
feedback.D: Incorrect. Multiplying by 4 inverts the cycle relationship. One cycle spans one-fourth of the total 10.0 cm distance, not 4 times the total distance.

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Calculating the time-base setting: "Dividing the period by the horizontal span of one cycle gives the time-base setting."
title: Calculating Time-Base Setting from Known Wave Parameters
action: Select the correct time-base setting in s cm^-1 when a sound wave of frequency 2000 Hz displays 1 cycle spanning 5.0 cm on the graticule.
prompt: A sound wave of frequency 2000 Hz is displayed on an oscilloscope. One complete wave cycle spans 5.0 cm horizontally on the graticule. What is the time-base setting of the oscilloscope?

options.text: 1.0 x 10^-4 s cm^-1, calculated from T = 1 / 2000 = 5.0 x 10^-4 s and time-base = (5.0 x 10^-4 s) / 5.0 cm.
400 s cm^-1, calculated by dividing frequency 2000 Hz by 5.0 cm.
2.5 x 10^-3 s cm^-1, calculated by multiplying period 5.0 x 10^-4 s by 5.0 cm.
1.0 x 10^4 cm s^-1, calculated by dividing 5.0 cm by period 5.0 x 10^-4 s.

feedback.A: Correct. First calculate period T = 1 / f = 1 / 2000 s^-1 = 5.0 x 10^-4 s. Then divide period by horizontal distance: time-base = (5.0 x 10^-4 s) / 5.0 cm = 1.0 x 10^-4 s cm^-1.
feedback.B: Incorrect. This divides frequency directly by distance. Frequency is cycles per second, not seconds. You must first invert frequency to find period in seconds.
feedback.C: Incorrect. Time-base represents time per unit distance (s cm^-1), which requires dividing period by distance, not multiplying.
feedback.D: Incorrect. This computes distance per unit time (speed in cm s^-1) rather than the oscilloscope time-base setting in seconds per centimetre (s cm^-1).

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Adjusting oscilloscope controls: "Adjusting the oscilloscope controls changes only the scale of the display and never alters the physical signal."
title: Predicting Waveform Changes from Oscilloscope Control Adjustments
action: Select the option that correctly describes the visual changes to a displayed trace when the time-base setting is increased from 0.1 ms cm^-1 to 0.5 ms cm^-1 and the y-gain is unchanged.
prompt: An oscilloscope displays three complete sinusoidal cycles across the screen. The time-base setting is now increased from 0.1 ms cm^-1 to 0.5 ms cm^-1 while keeping the input signal and y-gain unchanged. What happens to the displayed trace?

options.text: The trace compresses horizontally so that more complete cycles fit across the screen, while the vertical height remains unchanged.
The trace stretches horizontally so that fewer cycles appear on the screen, while the vertical height remains unchanged.
The trace increases in vertical height because a larger time-base amplifies the signal voltage.
The physical frequency of the wave decreases because the time-base knob slows down the incoming oscillations.

feedback.A: Correct. Increasing the time-base setting means each centimetre represents 5 times as much time. Therefore, 5 times as many cycles fit across the screen, compressing the trace horizontally.
feedback.B: Incorrect. Increasing the time-base setting represents more elapsed time across the same screen width, which compresses the trace horizontally rather than stretching it.
feedback.C: Incorrect. The time-base control scales only the horizontal time axis. It has no effect on the vertical voltage sensitivity, which is controlled solely by the y-gain.
feedback.D: Incorrect. Oscilloscope controls alter only the display scale on the screen. Adjusting an instrument knob never changes the physical frequency or amplitude of the incoming wave.

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Deriving the wave equation: "Substituting this period into the speed equation proves that wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength."
title: Physical Logic of the Wave Equation Derivation
action: Select the statement that correctly explains why v = f lambda follows directly from kinematics and wave definitions.
prompt: Which statement correctly describes the physical derivation of the wave equation v = f lambda for a progressive wave?

options.text: In one oscillation period T, the wave profile advances forward by one wavelength lambda; using v = distance / time gives v = lambda / T, and substituting T = 1/f yields v = f lambda.
Each particle of the medium travels forward along the direction of wave motion by distance lambda in time T, giving speed v = lambda / T = f lambda.
Because wave speed equals distance divided by time, v = T / lambda, and substituting f = 1/T yields v = f lambda.
The wave equation is an empirical rule observed in laboratories that cannot be derived from kinematics definitions.

feedback.A: Correct. In one period T, the wave disturbance travels a distance of one wavelength lambda. By definition of speed, v = lambda / T. Substituting the definition of frequency (T = 1/f) gives v = lambda / (1/f) = f lambda.
feedback.B: Incorrect. Particles of the medium do not travel forward with the wave. They vibrate in place about fixed equilibrium positions. It is the wave disturbance that advances by distance lambda.
feedback.C: Incorrect. Speed is defined as distance divided by time (lambda / T), not time divided by distance (T / lambda).
feedback.D: Incorrect. The wave equation is a rigorous theoretical deduction derived directly from the fundamental definitions of speed, wavelength, and frequency.

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Applying the wave equation > Worked Example 4: Calculating wavelength across wave types: "Always convert all metric prefixes into base SI units before performing calculations."
title: Applying the Wave Equation with Metric Prefixes
action: Select the correct wavelength of a microwave signal travelling at 3.00 x 10^8 m s^-1 with a frequency of 12 GHz.
prompt: A microwave radar signal travels through air at 3.00 x 10^8 m s^-1. The transmitter operates at a frequency of 12 GHz. What is the wavelength of the microwave radiation?

options.text: 0.025 m (or 2.5 cm), calculated from lambda = (3.00 x 10^8 m s^-1) / (12 x 10^9 Hz).
2.5 x 10^7 m, calculated by dividing 3.00 x 10^8 m s^-1 by 12 without converting gigahertz.
4.0 x 10^10 m, calculated from lambda = v x f = (3.00 x 10^8) x (12 x 10^9).
0.040 m, calculated by dividing frequency 12 x 10^9 Hz by speed 3.00 x 10^8 m s^-1.

feedback.A: Correct. Convert 12 GHz to 12 x 10^9 Hz. Rearranging v = f lambda gives lambda = v / f = (3.00 x 10^8 m s^-1) / (12 x 10^9 Hz) = 0.025 m = 2.5 cm.
feedback.B: Incorrect. This calculation forgets the giga- prefix (10^9). Without prefix conversion, the calculated wavelength is off by nine orders of magnitude.
feedback.C: Incorrect. This multiplies speed by frequency. Rearranging v = f lambda to solve for wavelength requires dividing speed by frequency: lambda = v / f.
feedback.D: Incorrect. This inverts the algebraic rearrangement by computing f / v instead of v / f.

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Synthesizing CRO traces with wave calculations > Worked Example 5: Combining a CRO trace with wave speed: "Multiplying the wave speed by the measured period gives the physical wavelength."
title: Synthesizing Oscilloscope Traces with Wave Speed
action: Select the correct physical wavelength of a sound wave travelling at 340 m s^-1 whose oscilloscope trace displays 2.0 cycles across 4.0 cm with a time-base setting of 0.25 ms cm^-1.
prompt: A microphone detects a sound wave travelling through air at 340 m s^-1. On a CRO screen, two complete cycles span a horizontal distance of 4.0 cm. The time-base setting is 0.25 ms cm^-1. What is the physical wavelength of the sound wave?

options.text: 0.17 m, calculated from period T = (2.0 cm x 0.25 x 10^-3 s cm^-1) = 5.0 x 10^-4 s and lambda = v T = 340 m s^-1 x 5.0 x 10^-4 s.
0.020 m, by assuming the 2.0 cm graticule length of one cycle on the screen is the physical wavelength.
0.34 m, calculated by using the total horizontal span of both cycles without dividing by 2.
6.8 x 10^5 m, calculated from lambda = v / T instead of lambda = v T.

feedback.A: Correct. One cycle spans 4.0 cm / 2 = 2.0 cm. Period T = 2.0 cm x 0.25 ms cm^-1 = 0.50 ms = 5.0 x 10^-4 s. Using lambda = v T gives lambda = 340 m s^-1 x 5.0 x 10^-4 s = 0.17 m.
feedback.B: Incorrect. The horizontal distance on a CRO screen represents time, not space. 2.0 cm on the graticule is a display dimension that must be converted to seconds via the time-base before calculating spatial wavelength.
feedback.C: Incorrect. This uses the 4.0 cm span of two complete cycles as the period of one cycle, doubling the true wavelength.
feedback.D: Incorrect. Since v = f lambda and f = 1 / T, wavelength is lambda = v / f = v T. Dividing speed by period is dimensionally incorrect.
